title: Read a bank statement (deposits, withdrawals, debit, fees, running balance) and keep a balance from a list of transactions

lesson.title: Reading a Bank Statement: Keeping the Running Balance

steps.say: You already know how to build a budget with money in and money out. A bank statement is that same idea, but it is real and it happens in order, one transaction at a time. The running balance is the column that answers the question you actually care about: how much money do I have right now?

Here are the words you will see on a statement. A deposit is money coming in, like your part time pay or allowance. A withdrawal is cash you take out at an A T M. A debit is when you tap your card at a store. A fee is what the bank charges you, like a monthly account fee. Only the deposit adds to your balance. The other three all take money out, even the tiny fee.

visual.caption: Four kinds of lines on a statement. Only the deposit column puts money in.

steps.say: Let us walk through a real week. You start with one hundred twenty dollars. Friday your part time pay of forty-five dollars goes in, so the balance becomes one hundred sixty-five. Saturday you tap your card for eighteen seventy-five on bubble tea with friends, and the balance drops to one hundred forty-six twenty-five. Then the bank takes its two fifty monthly fee, leaving one hundred forty-three seventy-five. Finally you pull forty dollars from an A T M, and you end at one hundred three seventy-five. Notice each new balance is built from the balance right before it.

visual.caption: Top row: the amount on each line. Bottom row: the running balance right after it.

steps.say: Two mistakes show up all the time. First, some people just add every number in the table together and get two hundred twenty-six twenty-five. That cannot be right, because money you spent does not make you richer. Second, some people skip the fee because it looks small, and they get one hundred six twenty-five. But the bank really did take that two fifty, so your true balance is one hundred three seventy-five. Every single line changes the balance, and money out always subtracts.

visual.caption: Only the last column matches what the bank actually holds for you.

steps.say: Many apps show money out as negative numbers, like minus eighteen seventy-five. Adding a negative is the same as subtracting, so the balances come out exactly the same as before. Here is the one that trips people up. Suppose the bank reverses a wrong twelve dollar charge. That means it removes a minus twelve from your account. Removing a negative puts the money back, so your balance goes up from one hundred three seventy-five to one hundred fifteen seventy-five. It does not go down to ninety-one seventy-five.

visual.caption: Running balance with signed amounts. The reversal removes a negative, so the balance rises.

steps.say: So here is the whole idea in one line. Read a statement top to bottom, and for every line ask: money in or money out? Deposits add, everything else subtracts, and your new balance always grows out of the one just above it.

lesson.answer: Money in adds, money out subtracts, and every line, even a tiny fee, updates the running balance.

practice.question: Maya's bank statement starts with an opening balance of eighty-five dollars. Then, in order: a deposit of sixty dollars from her part time job, a debit of twenty-three dollars and forty cents at the movies, a monthly account fee of three dollars and ninety-five cents, and an e-transfer out of thirty dollars to a friend. Draw a table with two rows: the amount on each line, and the running balance after it. What is the balance after each line, and what is Maya's final balance?
practice.answer: After the deposit: 145.00. After the movies: 121.60. After the fee: 117.65. After the e-transfer: 87.65. Final balance: 87.65 dollars.
